result.topic_en: Hilbert discusses when a polynomial f(x) splits modulo powers of a prime p in the same way as modulo p, notes that this fails when p divides the discriminant, and begins a proof using a Galois field, a prime ideal of p and the subfield attached to the group of substitutions fixing that prime ideal.

items.quote:
Man wird gut thun die Kronecker-
sche Fundamentalgleichung des Körpers zu

jedenfalls die Sätze in wiefern Functionen

items.english: One would do well to take Kronecker's fundamental equation of the field as the basis, and then one needs in any case the theorems on the extent to which functions are uniquely decomposable modulo powers of primes.
The theorem just mentioned turns out to be incorrect in general; namely, it holds only when p does not divide the discriminant.

items.quote:
Ist $f(x)$ nach $p$ in $\nu$ irreducible Faktoren zerlegbar, so ist
$f(x)$ nach [-...-] jeder Potenz von $p$ in ebensoviel Faktoren
zerlegbar, ausser wenn $p$ ein Teiler der Discriminante
ist und diese Eigenschaft charakterisirt auch wahr-
scheinlich umgekehrt die Teiler der Discriminante.
items.english: If f(x) is decomposable modulo p into ν irreducible factors, then f(x) is decomposable modulo every power of p into equally many factors, except when p is a divisor of the discriminant; and conversely this property probably also characterizes the divisors of the discriminant.

Suppose now that p is a prime that divides the discriminant, and that 𝔭 is a prime ideal of p. Then a certain power 𝔭^ν will be such that, if one takes the partial norm N𝔭^ν = 𝔭^ν 𝔭'^ν ⋯ 𝔭^{(μ−1)ν} with respect to a certain subfield V of degree μ, it becomes equal to p.

items.english: Now we prove the theorem: if a number α becomes congruent to a number in V modulo every power of 𝔭, then it is itself a number in V.
